title: How Does the Internet Actually Work?
summary: Explains the internet as a physical network of cables linking computers, the client/server roles, and the path a request takes when you type a domain name: browser → ISP → DNS server → IP address → direct request to the server, which sends back the site's files. Ends with a hands-on DNS lookup and a look at the undersea cables that carry the traffic.

concepts.heading: The internet is physical wiring
points: Strip away the 'cloud' image: the internet is a very large set of wires (copper and fibre) joining computers together so they can exchange data, for example a machine in London talking to one in Seattle.
It is the same idea as wiring two computers together, scaled up to every connected computer on the planet.

concepts.heading: Servers and clients
points: Server: a computer whose job is to stay online around the clock and hand out the files and data a website needs whenever someone asks for them.
Client: any computer (laptop, phone, etc.) that a person uses to go online and request those files.
A server can be pictured as a library that never closes: you ask for a page (Google's home page, the latest articles on a news site) and it supplies everything needed to display it.
The catch is scale: with so many sites stored on so many machines, the client needs a way to find the exact machine that holds the site it wants. DNS and IP addresses solve that.

concepts.heading: What happens when you type google.com
points: 1. The browser sends the request to your ISP (Internet Service Provider), the company you pay for access. Examples given: AT&T or Comcast in the US, BT or TalkTalk in the UK.
2. The ISP passes the domain name on to a DNS server. DNS stands for Domain Name System.
3. The DNS server works like an enhanced phone book: it looks up the domain name in its database and finds the matching IP address.
4. The IP address travels back through the ISP to your browser.
5. The browser now sends a request straight to that IP address. The machine living there (Google's servers) responds with all the files and data needed to show the page.
Every computer on the internet has an IP address. It acts like a postal code: a unique location that lets other computers find it to send or receive files.
(Extra) In practice your computer and ISP cache DNS answers, so repeat visits often skip the lookup. The request to the server uses HTTP/HTTPS, which the next lecture builds on.

(Extra) Many sites share a single IP (shared hosting, CDNs). The browser includes the domain name in its request (the Host header) so the server knows which site to return. That is why pasting a bare IP into the address bar does not work for every site.

concepts.heading: Try it: see a domain's IP address
points: Go to nslookup.io, enter google.com, and it lists the IP address(es) the DNS returns for Google.
Copy one of those IPs into a new browser tab: the Google home page loads, which repeats by hand what the browser normally does automatically after the DNS lookup.

concepts.heading: How data crosses oceans
points: Continents are joined by enormous submarine (undersea) cables. submarinecablemap.com shows every one of them and which reach your country.

Each cable bundles hundreds of optical fibres; lasers send the data as light pulses. The lecture quotes up to 400 gigabytes per second per fibre and shows a cross-section of a cable that lands in New Zealand.
Because the signals travel at close to light speed, a request can go halfway round the world and back in milliseconds. All the browser needs to start that journey is the server's IP address.

code_examples.caption: (Extra) The same DNS lookup from a terminal instead of nslookup.io
code_examples.code:
# Ask DNS for google.com's IP address(es)
nslookup google.com

# Shorter output, just the addresses
dig +short google.com

# See the chain of routers your packets pass through on the way
traceroute google.com     # macOS / Linux
tracert google.com        # Windows

code_examples.caption: (Extra) The request flow as a text diagram
code_examples.code:
You type google.com
   |
   v
Browser --("where is google.com?")--> ISP --> DNS server
                                            | looks up name
                                            v
Browser <------- IP e.g. 142.250.x.x ---- ISP
   |
   +--(request sent directly to that IP)--> Google's server
   <--(HTML, CSS, JS, images)-------------- Google's server

task.name: Try-it: look up an IP address and visit it
task.goal: See for yourself that a domain name is just a label for an IP address.
steps: Type google.com and run the lookup.
Copy one of the IPv4 addresses from the results.
Paste it into a new browser tab's address bar and press Enter.
Optional: open submarinecablemap.com and find the cables that land in your country.
task.expected_result: The Google home page loads from the raw IP address, showing that DNS just converts names into addresses.

pitfalls: Thinking of the internet as wireless or 'in the sky'; it is mostly cables, including under the sea.
Mixing up the roles: DNS only translates the name into an IP address; the actual files come from the web server at that address.
(Extra) Expecting every site to load from its bare IP. Sites on shared hosting or behind a CDN usually show an error or a certificate warning that way.

playground.coverage: The animated five-step demo covers typing a URL, the DNS lookup turning the name into an IP, the browser requesting files from the server, the server replying, and the browser rendering. The client/server labels are present.
gaps_and_ideas: Add the ISP hop the course shows: browser → ISP → DNS → back via ISP → direct request to the IP. The current demo jumps straight from browser to DNS.
Explain the IP address as the computer's postal code in the step 2 readout, and say every connected computer has one.
Add a 'Try it' task: look up google.com on nslookup.io and paste the IP into a new tab. Include a note that this fails for many CDN-hosted sites and why (Host header).
